elements.selection: All four Balmer lines between 400 and 700 nm.
The two D lines, which give a sodium lamp, and a flame that holds sodium, their yellow colour. NIST lists other, weaker lines of the neutral atom between 400 and 700 nm.

selectionSupport.where: The heading of the page's first section. Under it: the two D lines (588.9950 nm and 589.5924 nm, an electron falling from 3p to 3s) outshine every other line of sodium; the brightest visible line besides them has under one percent of the stronger D line's intensity, so that for practical purposes the light of glowing sodium is the D lines' light. A later section of the same page compares a sodium doublet with the spectrum of a sodium lamp. The page gives no colour. Read on 2026-10-17, after asking for the site's robots file, which it does not have.

Under the page's photographs of the flames of sodium chloride, strontium chloride and a barium mineral: the sodium flame looks the colour of other sodium lights, and its light comes mainly from the D lines. The flame test lab read the page on 2026-10-08; it was fetched again on 2026-10-17 and was the same file (the hash the flame test lab's manifest records). The page gives no colour in words.

The section on the lamp's history: the first low-pressure sodium lamps gave light very nearly of one colour, about the two sodium lines at these wavelengths in nanometres, and the article calls that light yellow. The caption of the spectrum of a low-pressure lamp calls its bright yellow band the D-line emission of the sodium atom. The opening paragraph calls the light of the low-pressure lamp yellow-orange.

elements.note: Both lines come from an electron falling from the 3p subshell to the 3s subshell. The 3p level is split into two levels very close in energy, so there are two lines. They are 0.6 nm apart, too close to draw separately on this strip, which shows them as one.

superseded.correction: These six lines are no longer shown. They were picked by hand on 2026-10-03 as the six strongest by NIST's relative intensity, and the sentence below said so. They are in fact the six with the largest transition probability, the column Aki (s^-1) that stands next to the relative intensity in NIST's table: the six numbers recorded here, 1.91e+06 to 5.83e+06, are transition probabilities, and until 2026-10-08 this file named them relativeIntensityAsPublished. Two of the six, at 467.12258 and 462.42756 nm, have no relative intensity in NIST's table at all. This was found on 2026-10-08, when one rule was applied to every element from saved copies of NIST's responses (docs/research/emission-spectra/). Since that day xenon's lines are the ones that rule picks, by relative intensity, on the periodic table and in the molecule explorer alike. The entry is kept as the record of what was shown before; the build reads nothing from it but this mark.

elements.selection: The six strongest lines of the neutral atom between 400 and 700 nm, by the relative intensity NIST lists. NIST lists several hundred xenon lines, and a real lamp also shows lines of the xenon ion.
